assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators, the quantum spin Hall state and the quantum anomalous Hall effect opened a new class of quantum matter, defined by band topology and protected edge states. It changed how band structure and spin-orbit coupling are understood, and it is tied tightly to first-principles electronic-structure calculations and measured spectra. It is a clear case where theory and experiment reinforced each other.
assessment.attribution: Kane supplies the decisive theory of the Z2 quantum spin Hall state, Molenkamp the first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, and Xue the experimental realization of the quantum anomalous Hall effect. This is a fair three-person split. Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal are not in this entry's credit list, so the allocation is contested and incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: more than fifteen years of independent confirmation across HgTe, Bi-based and magnetically doped materials, with quantized transport and ARPES agreeing with DFT-based predictions. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Credit for the 3D topological insulator and the original graphene-based proposal (Mele) is contested, and this entry omits those names.
I recall that the quantum anomalous Hall quantization was reproduced independently, but I have not verified the details here.
Practical impact is still prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the first controlled, nonperturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, exact in infinite dimensions. It explains the Mott transition and, combined with DFT, gives quantitative predictions for real correlated materials. It underlies much of modern computational materials theory, which is close to my own field.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar built the mapping to a quantum impurity problem, and Kotliar developed the DFT+DMFT extension. Muller-Hartmann and Jarrell are also relevant, but only the listed three can be proposed. The three names give a defensible but not clean configuration, because Metzner is absent.
assessment.maturity: Mature: about thirty years of use, broad cross-validation against experiment and against numerical benchmarks, with ongoing methodological refinement. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is a method rather than a discovery of a physical phenomenon may weigh against it with some members.
Credit among Metzner, Vollhardt, Georges, Kotliar and others is unresolved.
Accuracy of DMFT for low-dimensional systems is limited by its local approximation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire materials as a platform for correlated insulators, superconductivity and tunable quantum matter. A theoretical prediction of flat bands was followed by clear experimental discovery, which is the kind of theory-experiment pairing I value. It has founded a large new field.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero led the experimental discovery of correlated insulator and superconducting states. The three names form a natural configuration. Other work (for example on twisted-bilayer band structure by other groups) may deserve consideration but is outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Fairly young (2018 onward) but quickly reproduced by many independent groups. The phenomenology is still developing and the mechanism of superconductivity is not settled, so there is some risk of premature recognition.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism for superconductivity is unresolved.
Sample-dependent behaviour and reproducibility between devices remain concerns.
Whether the field has matured enough for a prize is a judgment call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. They enable tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. The discovery is clean, quantitative and heavily validated, which appeals to my emphasis on reproducibility.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first clocks; Ye drove the performance to record precision and many-body (spin-correlation) effects. The two-name credit is clear and fair. Other contributors are not in this credit list.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with multiple independent clocks agreeing at the 1e-18 level and international comparisons. Recognition is timely, since the redefinition of the second is being discussed.
uncertainties: Hall and Haensch already received the 2005 prize for the frequency comb that underlies the clocks, so a committee may see overlap.
Ye's credit also overlaps with other candidates, such as ultracold molecules.
This is outside my deepest expertise, so I defer to colleagues in atomic physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions are topological spin textures that are stable and can be manipulated by small currents. They connect to Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya physics, which I know well from first-principles magnetism calculations. They link fundamental topology to possible spintronic uses.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer and colleagues (Muhlbauer et al.) observed the skyrmion lattice in MnSi, Wiesendanger's group demonstrated individual skyrmions in atomically thin films, and Tokura contributed real-space imaging and materials discovery. Bogdanov's theoretical prediction is not in this entry's credit list, which leaves the allocation incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature, with many independent confirmations in bulk and multilayer systems, but room-temperature device applications are still unproven.
uncertainties: Missing theoretical credit (Bogdanov) weakens the configuration.
Technological payoff is not yet demonstrated.
Overlap of the three names' contributions is not cleanly separable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped-ion quantum computation combines the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal with high-fidelity experimental demonstrations of entangling gates and small algorithms. It is a foundational platform for quantum information processing. Its quantum-mechanical content is strong and it fits the theme that quantum mechanics keeps producing surprises.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the ion-trap quantum computer; Blatt realised many of the key experimental demonstrations. Wineland and Monroe are also major contributors, with Wineland already honoured in 2012, so the allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense of the basic gate, but scalable fault-tolerant computation is not yet shown. The 2012 prize already honoured ion manipulation.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for ion control.
Unclear whether the discovery is the scheme or the experimental platform.
Same three names appear in another candidate on the list, so the choice between entries is partly arbitrary.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spin-orbit torques enable electrical switching of magnetization without an external spin-polarized current, and have led to efficient memory concepts. The physics involves Rashba and spin Hall effects that I model with DFT. It is a genuine physical mechanism with technological relevance.
assessment.attribution: Miron and Gambardella demonstrated Rashba-based switching, Buhrman demonstrated spin Hall switching. The distinction between the spin Hall effect and Rashba contributions makes the credit allocation harder. Other pioneers of the spin Hall effect are not in this entry.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature, with many reproductions, but the microscopic split between mechanisms is still debated.
uncertainties: Relative roles of bulk spin Hall and interfacial Rashba mechanisms remain contested.
Credit is divided and the larger spin Hall literature is outside the list.
Commercial impact is still emerging.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism is a proposed third class of collinear magnetism with compensated order but spin-split bands. It is conceptually fresh and directly connected to magnetism and electronic-structure theory, which is my area, and ARPES data have followed predictions. It could be a significant finding in magnetism.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth formulated the symmetry classification and predictions; experimental confirmation came from other groups, who are not in the credit list. The three names are the theoretical core, but experimental credit is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Likely premature: only a few years since the 2022 classification and experimental verification is still limited, so recognition is early.
uncertainties: Independence and breadth of experimental confirmation are not yet established.
Earlier related ideas by other authors may complicate priority.
Practical relevance is speculative.
